## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Write regular expressions with `stringr`, from literal matches to
  groups.
- Extract structured fields, such as dates and dollar amounts, from
  messy text.
- Count word frequencies in a set of documents after dropping stop
  words.
- Score each document with a sentiment dictionary by counting its
  positive and negative words.
- Pair every pattern with a should-match test and a should-not-match
  test.

## What we cover {#coverage}

- [Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw024)
  built a keyword index, the monthly share of newspaper articles with a
  term from each of three lists (economy, policy, uncertainty), and had
  people read 12,000 articles to confirm it tracks policy uncertainty.
  [Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdab094)
  scored the tone of Fed meeting transcripts with a finance word list,
  compared the scores with research assistants' ratings of a sample, and
  estimated the Fed's implicit inflation target at about 1.5 percent.
  [Djourelova (AER, 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20211537) counted
  articles with the phrase "illegal immigrant" before and after the
  Associated Press banned it, and found that exposed readers grew less
  supportive of restrictive immigration policy.
- `stringr` and regular expressions (regex), written patterns that
  describe the text to find: literals, character classes (a set in
  brackets, any one of which can match, such as `[0-9]`), quantifiers
  (how often the piece before may repeat, such as `+` for one or more),
  anchors (`^` and `$` pin the start and the end) and groups.
- Extracting fields with capture groups, the parts of a pattern inside
  parentheses that come out as their own column. Each pattern carries
  should-match and should-not-match tests, strings it must catch and
  strings it must skip, rerun after every change. A row caught by
  mistake is a false positive; one missed is a false negative.
- The corpus: the Federal Reserve's policy statements and
  press-conference transcripts, provided as a file.
- Counting words: split each document in the corpus (the full set of
  documents you analyze) into tokens, usually single words, tabulate
  with `table()`, drop stop words such as "the" and "of", and compare
  term frequencies (a word's share of the document's words).
- Dictionary sentiment: a published list of positive and negative
  words, a count of each per document, and a net tone score (positive
  minus negative, over the word count). A dictionary built for one
  domain misreads another; "liability" and "tax" carry no sentiment in
  a company report. A human audit reads the top- and bottom-scoring
  documents and a random sample by hand to verify the score matches a
  person's judgment.
- Readability metrics in one slide, and a one-line fix for a broken
  character encoding, the rule that stores letters as numbers ("café"
  read with the wrong rule shows up as "cafÃ©").
- Regex and word counts are cheap and give the same answer on every
  run, which makes them the first thing to try on a new corpus.
